chunks: "An ISA, instruction set architecture, is the interface between software and the processor hardware.

It defines everything a programmer or compiler needs to know to write correct code for that CPU: the set of instructions and their binary encodings, the registers, the data types, how memory is addressed, how loads and stores behave, and how interrupts and exceptions work.
The important point is that it's a contract. Software only depends on the ISA, and the hardware team is free to implement it however it likes.
That's why the same ARMv8-A program runs on a tiny in-order core and a big out-of-order one, and why x86 binaries from decades ago still run on new chips.
The implementation is the microarchitecture. There are different styles.
RISC ISAs like Arm and RISC-V have simple, mostly fixed-length instructions, lots of registers and a load/store model where only loads and stores touch memory.
CISC like x86 has variable-length instructions and complex ones that can operate directly on memory.
For example in RISC-V, add x3, x1, x2 is a 32-bit word, 0x002081B3, with fields for the opcode, destination register and two source registers.
Compilers target the ISA, and the choice of ISA affects code density, decoder complexity, power, ecosystem and licensing."
